research_page.title: Blood Biomarkers to Detect Alzheimer Disease in Primary and Secondary Care (JAMA 2024)
research_page.description: A prospective study showing the APS2 blood test achieves 88-92% diagnostic accuracy for Alzheimer's pathology, outperforming standard clinical evaluations.
research_page.authors_line_md: Palmqvist et al. — Skane University Hospital
research_page.takeaway_md: The APS2 blood test (combining p-tau217 and Aβ42/40 ratios) accurately detects Alzheimer's disease pathology in approximately 90% of patients with cognitive symptoms. It significantly outperforms standard diagnostic evaluations by both primary care physicians and dementia specialists, highlighting its potential to dramatically improve and streamline Alzheimer's diagnosis in routine practice.
key_findings_md: The APS2 blood test demonstrated 88% to 92% diagnostic accuracy for Alzheimer's pathology across primary and secondary care cohorts (JAMA abstract).
Standard clinical evaluation yielded a diagnostic accuracy of only 61% for primary care physicians and 73% for dementia specialists, compared to 91% using the APS2 test (JAMA abstract).
The percentage of p-tau217 alone achieved a diagnostic accuracy of 90%, showing no statistical difference from the combined APS2 score (JAMA abstract).
research_page.methods_md: A prospective cohort study of 1,213 patients (mean age 74.2 years, 48% women) undergoing clinical evaluation for cognitive symptoms in primary and secondary care settings in Sweden. The study ran from February 2020 to January 2024, evaluating predefined cutoff values for the APS2 blood test.
research_page.trial_evidence_md: This paper reports findings from the Swedish BioFINDER primary care ([NCT06120361](/trials/biofinder-primary-care-nct06120361)) and secondary care ([NCT03174938](/trials/biofinder-2-nct03174938)) cohorts. The prospective evidence strongly supports the clinical utility of the APS2 biomarker (commercially available as PrecivityAD2) for detecting Alzheimer's pathology. The test is increasingly being integrated into both therapeutic endpoint strategies and dedicated diagnostic workflow trials.
research_page.sentiment_md: Public perception is overwhelmingly hopeful, heavily influenced by media headlines emphasizing the test's high accuracy over human doctors ([HealthDay News](https://www.healthday.com/health-news/neurology/blood-test-91-accurate-at-predicting-alzheimers-outperforming-doctors)). However, patient communities and the broader public frequently misinterpret the test as a standalone "lie-detector" for clinical dementia or an asymptomatic screening tool, rather than a measure of pathology that must be contextualized with observed cognitive symptoms.
caveats_md: The blood test detects the presence of underlying Alzheimer's pathology (amyloid and tau), which does not automatically equate to a clinical diagnosis of dementia without corresponding cognitive symptoms.
The available text is limited to the abstract, obscuring detailed methodological limitations, specific demographic diversity of the Swedish cohorts, and full financial disclosures of the authors.

trial_pages.title: BioFINDER - Primary Care
trial_pages.description: A prospective trial evaluating the diagnostic accuracy of the PrecivityAD2/APS2 blood test in primary care patients with mild cognitive symptoms.
trial_pages.population: Patients seeking medical care due to mild cognitive symptoms in primary care units.
trial_pages.primary_endpoint: Presence of brain AD pathology as determined by CSF AD biomarkers
trial_pages.why_md: This study evaluates whether blood-based biomarkers like the APS2 score can accurately detect Alzheimer's pathology in primary care settings, where access to specialized imaging or CSF tests is typically limited. It provides key real-world validation for integrating blood tests into frontline cognitive evaluations. See [Biomarkers](/research/biomarkers) for more context.
status_log_md: **2024-07-28** — JAMA publishes findings showing 88-92% diagnostic accuracy for the APS2 algorithm in the primary care cohort, outperforming standard physician evaluation. ([JAMA](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2024.13855))
trial_pages.results_md: A 2024 readout reported in JAMA demonstrated that the APS2 blood test achieved 88% to 92% diagnostic accuracy in the primary care cohort, compared to only 61% for standard clinical evaluation by primary care physicians.

trial_pages.title: BioFINDER 2
trial_pages.description: A large prospective study assessing blood and CSF biomarkers across healthy individuals and patients with cognitive symptoms in secondary care.
trial_pages.population: Healthy individuals, SCD/MCI, AD dementia, and other dementias evaluated in memory clinics (secondary care).
trial_pages.primary_endpoint: Clinical diagnosis according to consensus group decision blinded to the diagnostic test
trial_pages.why_md: This expansive cohort study aims to validate fluid and imaging biomarkers for Alzheimer's and related dementias in specialized memory clinic settings. It serves as a foundational dataset for comparing novel blood tests against gold-standard evaluations by dementia specialists.
status_log_md: **2024-07-28** — JAMA publishes findings showing the APS2 test achieved approximately 91% diagnostic accuracy in the secondary care cohort, significantly outperforming standard evaluation by dementia specialists. ([JAMA](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2024.13855))
trial_pages.results_md: In a 2024 JAMA publication, the APS2 blood test demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy (~91%) in the secondary care cohort, superior to the 73% diagnostic accuracy achieved by dementia specialists using standard clinical evaluation.
